country.comment: Single-country study examining the Kirindi Oya irrigation system in the southeastern dry zone of Sri Lanka.
country.where_found: PDF p. 1, Title and Abstract; PDF p. 3, Site description

effect_estimate.comment: The article synthesizes empirical fieldwork qualitatively and institutionally without reporting inferential statistics or quantitative effect estimates.
effect_estimate.value: Qualitative — no numeric effect estimate reported. Sectoral water agencies (>20 nationally, notably the Irrigation Department, National Water Supply and Drainage Board [NWS&DB], and Department of Wildlife Conservation), formal water rights, and user groups in Sri Lanka's Kirindi Oya irrigation system formally recognize only irrigated field crops and domestic drinking water, excluding homestead gardens, livestock watering, fisheries, small enterprises, and downstream wetlands from system-level allocation. Participatory irrigation bodies (59 Distributary Channel Organizations, 690 Field Channel Groups, and the joint government-user Project Management Committee [PMC]) restrict farmer membership to irrigated-land cultivators (predominantly men) and omit NWS&DB, Fisheries Cooperative Societies, Standpipe Committees, and wildlife authorities from the PMC. For domestic piped standposts (15–20 households per standpost; Rs 11/month fee), NWS&DB limits formal use to drinking and enforces collective disconnection plus a Rs 250 reconnection fee for violations alongside low supply reliability (a few variable hours/day), whereas informal user norms accommodate bathing, laundry, pilgrim, and small-enterprise water use when alternative sources are absent, and dry-season canal releases are issued once every 14 days for domestic bathing and laundry.
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF pp. 5–12, Tables 1–2 and Institutional environment / Accommodating multiple users sections

mechanism_certainty.comment: Rated 2 (mechanism directly observed) under the non-experimental design ceiling: primary fieldwork (direct observations at standpipes and tanks, focus groups, household surveys, and key informant interviews with agency officials and user-group leaders) directly documents how land-tied membership rules, sectoral agency mandates, standpost tariff/disconnection enforcement, administrative refusals, and informal local accommodation operate on water access across user groups.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF pp. 2–3, Introduction; PDF pp. 5–11, Institutional environment and Accommodating multiple users sections

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines land-tenure/property-tied irrigation water rights and FO membership eligibility as well as garden/hotel ineligibility and old-vs-new command-area priority (ELIGIBILITY: tenure, property, service_area); monthly standpost charges of Rs 11, Rs 250 reconnection fees, and tripled hotel water tariffs (BURDEN: fees); collective standpost disconnection and reconnection penalties for non-drinking use (ENFORCEMENT: disconnection, reconnection); and participatory user bodies/PMC gender and stakeholder exclusion, sectoral fragmentation across >20 agencies, political protest over dry-season reallocation, flexible seasonal planning, and informal local accommodation of non-drinking standpost and garden uses (DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION: discretion, accommodation, participation, institutional_fragmentation, political_coordination).
mechanism_flags.value: ELIGIBILITY, BURDEN, DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION, ENFORCEMENT, tenure, property, service_area, fees, discretion, accommodation, disconnection, reconnection, participation, institutional_fragmentation, political_coordination
mechanism_flags.where_found: PDF pp. 5–11, Tables 1–2 and Institutional environment / Accommodating multiple users sections; PDF p. 12, Note 5

outcome_flags.comment: Examines multi-use and domestic water access, low daily reliability and intermittent hours/dry-season scheduling at standposts and canals, water allocation quantities, water quality (measured across sources; salinity and agrochemical impacts), and administrative denial of surface-water abstraction requests by hotels and formal prohibition of garden withdrawals.
outcome_flags.value: water_access, service_reliability, service_continuity, service_quantity, service_quality, refusal
outcome_flags.where_found: PDF pp. 2–3, Introduction; PDF p. 5, Table 1; PDF pp. 6–8, Institutional environment; PDF p. 11, Accommodating multiple users

publication_year.comment: Published in Agriculture and Human Values, volume 16, pp. 281–293, in 1999 (accepted in revised form December 12, 1998).
publication_year.where_found: PDF p. 1, journal header and copyright notice

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: Primary interdisciplinary fieldwork explicitly combined quantitative components (stratified household survey of 156 households and water quality measurements across sources) with qualitative components (~10 focus group discussions, direct observations at standpipes and tanks, and key informant interviews), matching MMAT, although findings in this article are synthesized qualitatively/descriptively.

sample_size.comment: Exact counts are reported for the stratified household survey (78 households in each of the 2 areas = 156 households) and focus groups (~10), while exact numbers of water quality samples, direct observation sessions, and key informant interviews are not reported.
sample_size.value: 156 households (78 households in the old area and 78 households in the new area); about 10 focus group discussions; plus key informant interviews, direct observations at standpipes and tanks, and water quality measurements across system sources (exact counts not reported) within 1 irrigation system (Kirindi Oya)

study_design.comment: Interdisciplinary single-system case study combining primary quantitative data collection (stratified household survey and water quality measurements) and qualitative methods (direct observations, focus group discussions, and key informant interviews), with results synthesized qualitatively and institutionally in the article.
study_design.value: Mixed-methods single-case institutional study combining a stratified household survey, water quality measurements, direct observations, focus group discussions, and key informant interviews
